comments.text_zh: 我在机器学习方面是个新手，但 Open AI 做了一个用于电子游戏强化学习的 Python 库，它的一个 fork 仍在积极维护 [1]。已经过去几年了，但我记得当时能在一两天内（也许一个周末）把它跑起来。它用的是 Retroarch 模拟器，兼容大量模拟器和主机。[LINK] 还有 SethBling 在 YouTube 上关于机器学习的精彩视频，专门用 Super Mario World 来做：[VIDEO] 我鼓励你试一试！我觉得电子游戏在当前的 AI 热潮中有点被低估了，我认为机器通过玩游戏来学习技能有很大潜力。而选择甚至创造一款游戏，以教授特定技能为目标，也很有潜力。不过到了那个阶段，也许最好放弃音频和画面，用文本或纯数据与机器交流。另一方面，我看过一个关于卷积神经网络的视频，它直接以图像的每个像素为输入。所以也许用声音数据训练，或者用频谱图的像素训练，可能会有一些正面结果。而且我当然会很乐意看到一款游戏随着音乐节奏来玩，甚至可能伴着歌曲的旋律、和声和故事跳舞。人类创造过的一切，最初都存在于人脑的想象中。而你也有一个这样的大脑。追逐心中的愿景，并把它从头脑带入现实，是一件美好的事，
comments.text: I'm a novice at machine learning, but Open AI made a python library for reinforcement learning in video games, and a fork of it is still actively maintained [1]. It's been a few years, but I remember being able to get it up and running in a day or two (maybe a weekend). It used the Retroarch emulator, which is compatible with a huge number of emulators and consoles. [LINK] There also SethBling's excellent video on YouTube about machine learning specifically with Super Mario World: [VIDEO] I encourage you to give it a try! I feel that video games are a bit underrated by current AI buzz, I think there's lots of potential for a machine to learn a skill through playing a game. And lots of potential for a game being selected or even created with the goal of teaching a specific skill. However at that point maybe it's better to forego the audio and visuals and speak to the machine in text or with pure data. On the other hand, I have seen a video about convolutional neural networks that feed on each pixel of an image. So perhaps training with sound data, or with the pixels of a spectrogram, could have some positive results. And certainly I would be amused to see a game played in time with music, or possibly even dancing with a songs melody, harmony, and story as well. Anything that's ever been created by humans, existed first in the imagination of a human brain. And you've got one of those. A mental vision pursued and brought from the mind into physical reality is a beautiful thing,

comments.text: I believe it's been posted before, but sethbling (of vanilla-minecraft-hacks fame) pulled off the impossible and did the credit warp on an actual SNES, live[1]. As this video very-nicely explains, this required incredible amounts of pixel-perfect accuracy. Lining up the line of koopa shells on exact x-offsets and very narrow heights mid jump (!) to write the landing-sled - using a controller, realtime - is utterly insane. As a side note sethbling's latest project is teaching[2] (using neuro-evolution) his machine learning bot to play SMW[2], SMB1[3], and Mario Kart (original)[4]. While he machine learning is simple by today's standards, his brief videos give a really nice introduction to the topic that should be accessible to most people. comments.author: cookiengineer
comments.story_title: Ask HN: Is genetic programming still actively researched?
comments.why_zh: NEAT 概念的不错入门。
comments.quote_zh: 有个不错的入门视频，讲的是底层基础概念 NEAT
comments.text_zh: 遗传编程圈子某种程度上演化成了 NEAT、HyperNEAT 和 ES-HyperNEAT，作为一种元学习概念。层/节点之间的连接被序列化为智能体的基因，带有表型和显性/隐性标记，而一个负责观察的 CPPN 会学习把智能体归类到不同性状中，以找到更高效的繁殖机制。这是个很强的概念，而且据我所知，它在机器人领域仍被大量使用，因为出于安全法规，你必须保证行为可复现。有个不错的入门视频，讲底层基础概念 NEAT，是 youtuber SethBling 做的 [2]。就我而言，我把它用作去中心化学习方法，因为点对点网络可以从能通信、适应并自我学习的遗传 AI 中大大受益。[1] [LINK] [2] [VIDEO]
comments.text: The genetic programming scene kind of evolved into NEAT, HyperNEAT and ES-HyperNEAT as a meta learning concept. Connections between layers/nodes are serialized as genes of agents with phenotypes and dominant/recessive markers, and an observing CPPN learns to categorize agents into different traits to find more efficient breeding mechanisms. It's a strong concept, and AFAIK it's still used a lot in the robotics world where you have to guarantee behaviors and have to be able to reproduce behaviors due to safety regulations. There was a nice intro video into the underlying base concept which is called NEAT by a youtuber named SethBling [2] In my case I'm using this as a decentralized learning approach, because peer to peer networks can benefit heavily from genetic AIs that can communicate, adapt and learn from themselves. [1] [LINK] [2] [VIDEO]

comments.text_zh: 联结主义是心灵哲学中的一种进路，而且从近来深度学习的火热程度来看，它是最成功的一种进路。OP 里我觉得勉强算相关的唯一一本书是 Dennet 写的那本，而普遍认为那本书相当糟糕。有一个更有趣但有缺陷的进路，对热爱 Dawkins 和 Hitchens（无神论者、进化论拥护者）的人来说会有共鸣，那就是 Gerald Edelman 的 Neural Darwinism（1978）。甚至在 University of Texas 还有现代研究（是真实、可运行的代码）可以被视为 Edelman 的继承者：NeuroEvolution of Augmenting Topologies（NEAT）[VIDEO]
comments.text: connectionism is an approach to the philosophy of mind, the most successful approach as evidenced by recent deep learning hype the only book in the OP I thought was even mildly relevant was the one by Dennet, and it's generally acknowledged that it's pretty bad. A more interesting but flawed approach, that resonates as someone who loves Dawkins and Hitchens (atheists and advocates of evolution), is Gerald Edelman's Neural Darwinism (1978). There is even modern research (that is real, working code) at the University of Texas that could be considered a successor to Edelman: NeuroEvolution of Augmenting Topologies (NEAT) [VIDEO]

comments.text_zh: 感谢 togelius [1, 2] 和 deepnet [上文] 的评论。有人有兴趣给 Seth 的项目加一点学术味道吗？词语在不同语境下对不同人确实意味着不同的东西……近来有一批文献探讨现代“maker”[3] 运动。然而，“maker”这个说法可能并不太适合 OP 的论点[1]，后者把（学术）研究者与所谓的“修补匠”对立起来。“修补匠”的另一个说法可能是“bricoleur”，一个来自法语的外来词。（大致上，它仍指一个修补折腾的人：[LINK]，但根据学术视角不同，还有其他含义。）考虑到我们是在教育语境下讨论会玩的 AI，我们也可以回到 Seymour Papert 关于 [LINK] 的工作。AI 研究者 Papert 最初因与 Marvin Minsky 合著 _Perceptrons_ 而闻名，后来他把教育理论转向“在做中学”（learning-by-making）的愿景以及（年轻的）bricoleur [4]。这种做法可以从 1960 年代的图形 [turtle] [LINK] 到 Lego [LINK]，再到现代鼓励儿童编程的努力[5,6,7] 的演变中看出来。Papert 后来的合作者之一 Sherry Turkel 讨论了 bricolage 在编程中的应用——[LINK]。谈到早期教育，Turkel 主张认识论多元主义[8]，并引用人类学家 Levi-Strauss，把分析科学与“具体事物的科学”相比较。我们可以既欣赏 Seth Bling 的具体性[9]，也可以欣赏 Togelius 的原创论文……
comments.text: Thanks for the commentary togelius [1, 2] and deepnet [above]. Anyone interested in adding a soupçon of scholarship to Seth's project? Words do mean different things to different people, in different contexts.. There is a recent body of literature that explores the modern "maker" [3] movement. However, "maker" as a term may not have been a good fit for the OP's argument [1], which contrasted (academic) researchers with so-called "tinkerers". An alternative term for "tinkerer" might be "bricoleur", a loanword from French. (Roughly, it still means one who tinkers: [LINK] but has other meanings depending on the academic lens.) Given that we are discussing AIs that play, in the context of education, we can also go back to Seymour Papert's work on [LINK] . Originally known for work on _Perceptrons_ with Marvin Minsky, AI researcher Papert later adapted theories from education towards the vision of "learning-by-making" and the (young) bricoleur [4]. This can approach can be seen in the evolution from 1960s graphical [turtle] [LINK] to Lego [LINK] to modern day efforts to encourage coding-for-kids [5,6,7]. One of Papert's later collaborators, Sherry Turkel, discusses bricolage as it applies to programming -- [LINK] . When it comes to early education, Turkel argues for epistemological pluralism [8] and cites anthropologist Levi-Strauss in comparing analytic science with a "science of the concrete". comments.author: mockingbirdy
comments.story_title: Logic Theorist
comments.why_zh: AI 通过试错和奖励学习玩 Mario 的例子。
comments.text_zh: 如果你看 AI 学习跑步 [1] 或玩 Mario [2] 的视频，就会看到确实存在“随机瞎试，直到你的奖励函数给出正反馈”这种训练 AI 的方法。困难的部分是设计奖励函数。我们基于激素的激励系统里蕴含着大量智能——我们会感到疼痛、会感到悲伤等等。这些情绪中有许多是预先设定好的。如果我们找到一种方法，设计出目标正确的强化系统，我们就能像大自然母亲几十亿年来所做的那样做到这一点。但这仍然需要大量算力。如果我们把大自然看作一个大规模并行计算系统，它把“活下去”定义为奖励（不是因为它“想要”这样，而是因为这自然涌现出来），它就向我们展示了：如果我们试图构建一个获得智能的完全随机过程，我们需要多少算力。我认为你提出的方法（“随机拼装解并测试它们”）是可行的，因为我们已经在大自然中见过它。但不管我们的算力多强，它都需要大量时间和能量。我认为，当我们找到合适的边界和奖励函数，而不是随机尝试各种东西时，我们会更快。 [1]: [LINK] [2]: [VIDEO]
comments.text: If you watch videos of AIs learning to run [1] or playing Mario [2], you see that there's definitely "try random shit until your reward function gives you positive feedback" as a method for training AIs. The difficult part is developing the reward function. There's a lot of intelligence in our hormone-based incentive system - that we feel pain, that we feel sad, etc. Many of those emotions are pre-programmed. If we find a way to design reinforcement systems with the right goals, we can do it like mother nature did it for several billion years. But it's still a ton of computational power required. If we look at nature as a massively parallelized computational system that defined "just live" as the reward (not because it "wants" it, but because it just emerged), it shows us how much power we would need if we would try to build a completely random process that gains intelligence. I think your proposed method works ("just assemble random solutions and test them") because we've already seen it in nature. But it takes a lot of time and energy, regardless of our computational power. I think we're faster when we find the right boundaries and reward functions instead of randomly trying stuff.
